newsitem.title: USA: Navy survivors of atom test have higher death rate.
newsitem.headline: Navy survivors of atom test have higher death rate.

text.p: Navy personnel involved in 1946 nuclear tests at Bikini Atoll have died at a 4.6 percent higher rate than comparable U.S. sailors, but radiation did not appear to be the reason, the Institute of Medicine said in a report on Tuesday.
Some 40,000 military personnel, mostly from the Navy, participated in Operation Crossroads, the first of the U.S. above-ground nuclear detonations conducted at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands.

While these veterans' overall death rate was elevated, deaths from cancers and leukaemia -- expected to be higher if radiation was a cause -- were not statistically significant, said the study by the Medical Follow-Up Agency of the Institute of Medicine.
Even servicemen believed to have been exposed to the highest radiation doses did not die from unusually high rates of cancer or leukaemia, the study said.
Participants in Operation Crossroads boarded vessels that were covered with nuclear fallout, and tried to decontaminate the vessels by washing them down.
The study's director, Christopher Johnson, said its findings were in line with previous examinations of British and U.S. servicemen involved in nuclear tests.
Reasons for the higher death rate were unclear, the study said, but could be caused by an unknown factor related to the nuclear tests other than radiation.

Also, it said sailors who became ill may have sought to be included in the medical follow-up group, raising the mortality rate. But it said that would have a minor effect since nearly all participants have been studied.

This study funded by the Veterans Department and the Defence Special Weapons Agency was the first extensive review of death rates among this group of servicemen. It only examined mortality, not incidence of diseases.
The study used a roster of men who participated in the nuclear tests which was 96-98 percent complete.
For comparison, the institute established a control group of men who served in the military at the same time and in similar military units, but did not participate in Operation Crossroads.

"I'm not surprised they came up with a finding like that," said Oscar Rosen, past national commander of the National Association of Atomic Veterans, which has pushed for compensation of veterans of military nuclear testing.
"So many veterans are alive and still deserving of compensation, and this study doesn't help them a single bit," Rosen said.

He said he had not yet seen the study, but said it was inadequately funded by the Veterans Department and relied on death certificates that in many cases would not provide full information on contributing causes of death.
For instance, he said, often the cause of death for cancer patients is listed as heart or respiratory failure, he said.
